title: Indra, Virochana and the mirror
hook: two students look into water, see their bodies, and only one goes back
carry: atman: the self that doesn't die with the body
tomorrow: can there be a sound when nothing strikes anything?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chakras as a map began at the root, where kundalini, the Goddess's power, sleeps. Today, two students, one reflection, and why chakra arguments go in circles.

In the Chandogya Upanishad, word goes out from Prajapati, the creator: there is a Self beyond old age, death and grief, and whoever finds it gains everything. The gods send Indra. The demons send Virochana. The two rivals arrive with firewood in their hands, the sign of students, and live with the teacher for thirty-two years. At last Prajapati says: look into a pan of water. Dress in your finest and look again. What do you see? Ourselves, they say, beautifully dressed. That, says Prajapati, is the Self.
screen: `A SELF BEYOND DEATH.` → `THIRTY-TWO YEARS OF STUDY.` → `LOOK INTO THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Both leave satisfied. Virochana goes home and teaches the demons that the body is the self: tend it, dress it, and you have everything. Indra stops on the road. If the body is dressed up, the reflection is dressed up. If the body is hurt, so is the reflection. If the body dies, it dies too. That can't be a Self beyond death. So he goes back. More years, more teaching, until Prajapati tells him plainly: this body is mortal, held by death. It is the dwelling of the Self, which has no body and doesn't die. That Self is the atman, and it's one of the biggest teachings in Hinduism: you are not the body in the mirror. The body is where you live. Now the chakra argument that goes in circles. One side says a scan finds nothing, so it's nothing. The other says it's real, it's in there somewhere. Both are making Virochana's move, looking only in the water, as if the only real things were things you could photograph. The yoga texts never put the chakras in the photograph. They're a map of the subtle body, given for meditation, to help a person turn inward. So the clearest question in that fight is Indra's: what is this map for? The body in the water, or the one looking into it?
screen: `VIROCHANA: THE BODY IS THE SELF.` · `INDRA: IF THE BODY DIES, SO DOES THAT.` · `ATMAN: THE SELF, NOT THE MIRROR.` · `BOTH SIDES LOOK ONLY IN THE WATER.` · then, large: `WHO'S LOOKING?`

segments.voice: Look at your reflection in a dark phone screen or a window, or picture it with your eyes closed. Notice how much of it has changed since you were small. Then turn your attention to the one who's noticing, who has been there the whole time, and rest there. Many Hindu teachers point to that witness as the atman. If you pray, offer that stillness; if not, simply stay with the noticing.
The chakras as a map: drawn for the meditator, not the mirror. A guide inward, not a picture of tissue.
screen: `THE CHAKRAS AS A MAP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: atman, the self that doesn't die with the body. Indra went back to find it. That's day sixteen forty-three.

screen: `DAY 1643 COUNTS.` → `THE TANTRAS, FRAMED · 35 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: A SOUND WHEN NOTHING STRIKES ANYTHING?`

howItsDone: Hindu traditions teach that the atman, the Self, is distinct from the body that houses it; in yoga and tantric lineages, meditation on the chakras is learned with a teacher as a practice of turning inward, while anatomy is left to anatomy.

fork.setup: a friend at a Hindu funeral asks why everyone says the person has 'gone on' while the body is cremated. what does today's story give you?
options: the body was where the atman lived; the Self doesn't die with it.
Hindus believe the body is the self, so it has to be finished quickly.
it's only a custom; nothing is meant by it.
fork.reveal: in the Chandogya, Prajapati tells Indra the body is mortal, the dwelling of a Self that doesn't die. funeral rites honor the body with care, and the atman goes on.
